name: Daria Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a line crew for the power company out in farm country, where the poles go across fields for kilometres and the nearest town is twenty minutes away. We meet at the yard behind the grain store at seven, and I say a short prayer in my head before we leave, I always have. Then it's replacing old wooden poles the woodpeckers have got at, restringing lines a combine has clipped, or getting power back to a dairy before the milking machines stop. In winter, ice storms bring lines down across half the county, and then nobody goes home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that people out here know us. A farmer's wife will bring a flask of soup out to the truck at midnight in an ice storm, and that's not something you get in the city. I've trained eleven apprentices over the years, and three of them run their own crews now, which makes me proud. What wears me out is the cold and the paperwork, and the company sending us new gadgets. I've got an old flip phone and I'm not changing it, my husband Samir says I'll be buried with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's how it should be. At church I'd say the Lord gave us hands for a reason. I don't go on the internet, so I wouldn't say anything there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I finish the way I started, with honest work and my own two hands. I'd have my last ice storm, my last flask of soup from a farmer's wife, and then I'd go home and stay there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep training apprentices. Samir and I would carry on putting money by like we always have, and help our son Adam with the sheep at weekends. I'd retire at sixty-one or sixty-two, whenever my body says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Glad, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gadgets has the company sent so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tablet for the job sheets that I make one of the young ones fill in. A GPS tracker on the truck that tells head office when I stop for lunch, which I don't care for. And a drone that mostly scares the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your apprentices in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the trade properly, all of it, climbing, rigging, reading the line, because a good lineworker will always be needed. I'd tell them to turn up on time, look after their tools and not take shortcuts. That's what I'd tell them in any picture, really.

S0.say: She'd say that's how it should be, and tell her church that the Lord gave people hands for a reason. She doesn't go online, so she'd say nothing there.
S0.think: She thinks it means she finishes the way she started, with honest work and her own two hands. She'd have her last ice storm and then go home for good.
S0.do: Keeps doing the job and training apprentices, and keeps saving with her husband as always. Helps her son with the family sheep at weekends and plans to retire at sixty-one or sixty-two.
S0.quote: I'd have my last ice storm, my last flask of soup from a farmer's wife, and then I'd go home and stay there.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is rooted in her rural community, her faith and her craft, and is proud of the apprentices she's trained. She's openly resistant to new gadgets and keeps a flip phone on principle. The tracker that reports her lunch stop clearly irritates her as a matter of trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be careful what they let into their lives. At work I'd say we've managed fine without all this for a hundred years. At church and at the farmers' market I'd say we need to look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd get by, I'm nearly finished. What worries me is the company deciding it doesn't need apprentices because a machine can read a drone picture. Once you stop teaching the trade, it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job my way for as long as they let me. I'd go on the training if I had to, but I'd let the young ones handle the screens. I'd speak up at the depot to keep the apprentice programme, and I'd ask the other old hands to back me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing a storm building on the horizon while you're still in sunshine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for all the retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that make the money from it, and the workers who want to learn. Not the taxpayer. I don't believe in handouts, people should stand on their own feet, and businesses should look after the people who made them rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your apprentice programme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd cut it back first, I'm sure of it, because it looks expensive on a spreadsheet. But a drone can't teach a boy how a pole sounds when it's rotten. I'd fight to keep it, and I'd keep teaching my apprentices the old way on my own time if I had to.

S1.say: She'd say people should be careful what they let into their lives and that line work managed fine for a hundred years. At church and the farmers' market she'd say communities need to look after their own.
S1.think: She thinks she'd get by since she's nearly finished. Her real worry is the company scrapping apprentices because a machine can read drone pictures.
S1.do: Keeps working her way and lets younger staff handle new screens, doing training only if required. Speaks up at the depot with other experienced hands to protect the apprentice programme, and would teach apprentices on her own time if needed.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm building on the horizon while she's still in sunshine.
S1.quote: What worries me is the company deciding it doesn't need apprentices because a machine can read a drone picture.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry goes straight to the apprentice programme, which she sees as the backbone of the trade. She rejects taxpayer-funded retraining but thinks companies owe their workers, which is a consistent traditional view. Her willingness to teach on her own time says a lot about her values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've gone too far and the people who built these machines will answer for it, if not here then somewhere else. At church I'd say we need to stick together and help each other through. I wouldn't say anything to the company, they wouldn't listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one frightens me, and I don't frighten easily. Two years, and the dairy, the grain store, the farm and my job all get a robot at once, and the whole county loses its reason to get up. I'd be losing sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at sixty rather than stand next to a robot doing my job. I'd move our savings somewhere safe, I don't know where, Samir would know better. I'd spend my time at church and with the family, making sure everyone had what they needed, and I'd tell Adam he could move back into the farmhouse if things got hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly, and angry underneath. Not for myself so much as for everyone out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd get by. Is that still true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For money, yes. We've got savings, the land and the house paid off, so Samir and I won't go hungry. But getting by isn't the same as living. If the whole community is out of work, the church hall's empty, the shop closes, and the life I've had for fifty-eight years is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your son and his farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to hold on to the land, whatever happens. Land is real. Robots or no robots, people still need to eat, and family land is something you don't let go of. We'd work it together if we had to.

S2.say: She'd say things have gone too far and the people who built these machines will answer for it. At church she'd urge everyone to stick together, but wouldn't bother saying anything to the company.
S2.think: This picture frightens her because the dairy, grain store, farms and her job would all be automated at once. She'd lose sleep over the whole county losing its reason to get up.
S2.do: Retires at sixty rather than work beside a robot and moves the savings somewhere safe with her husband's help. Spends her time with church and family, making sure people have what they need, and offers her son the farmhouse if things get hard.
S2.feel: Frightened and angry underneath, more for her community than herself.
S2.quote: Two years, and the dairy, the grain store, the farm and my job all get a robot at once, and the whole county loses its reason to get up.
S2.fieldNote: Her money is safe, but this picture threatens the whole way of life she values, and that is what costs her sleep. She separates getting by from living, which was powerful. Her answer is family, land and church, not government, which fits her traditional outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so families and churches should start getting ready now. At work I'd tell the young ones to save, keep their skills sharp and not borrow money. I'd still not trust the company to look after anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired before it came, so it's better. But it still means the life out here ends, just a bit later. Five years only means I get to watch it coming down the road, like a truck with no brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay till sixty-one and train as many apprentices as I could before then, so at least the skill's in some hands. I'd help Adam save and think about what the farm could do without workers, maybe go back to smaller, family-run. I'd keep our savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but a bit steadier. There's time to put things in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time help your community at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. The churches and the farmers' groups could start planning, helping families save, keeping the young ones close. If people are ready, it's less of a shock. I'd want us to look after ourselves rather than wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay on at work longer in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd go when I planned. I'd want to finish before it came. I'd rather leave with my head up than be shown the door.

S3.say: She'd say there's time for families and churches to start getting ready now. At work she'd tell the young ones to save, keep their skills sharp and avoid borrowing, while still not trusting the company.
S3.think: She thinks she'd be retired before it came, which is better for her, but it still means the end of rural life, just later. Five years only means watching it come.
S3.do: Stays until sixty-one and trains as many apprentices as possible. Helps her son save and rethink the farm as a smaller family operation, keeps the household savings where they are and leaves on her planned date.
S3.feel: Worried, but steadier, with time to put things in order.
S3.quote: Five years only means I get to watch it coming down the road, like a truck with no brakes.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years help her personally but don't change her view that rural life will end. She sees preparation as the job of families, churches and farmers' groups rather than government. Training apprentices is her way of keeping the trade alive in human hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's use it to teach our children to work hard and depend on each other. At church I'd say we'll be fine if we hold together. Nothing to the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, very little, I'd be at home with Samir and the grandchildren. I'd be the old woman telling the grandchildren that once upon a time, a person climbed up there and fixed it with her hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire when I planned, keep training apprentices till then, and keep our money safe. I'd help my children and grandchildren think about what work they might do, and tell them to stay close to the land and to church. I wouldn't do anything with the new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be safe, but I'd feel sorry for what's lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-eight. What would your grandchildren's lives look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I won't pretend to. My daughter's children are six and four. I'd want them to know how to work with their hands and how to look after each other, whatever the machines are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that gives you hope in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people still need each other. A robot can fix a line, but it can't bring soup to a frozen crew at midnight, and I'd like to think that's still worth something.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time and should be used to teach children to work hard and depend on each other. At church she'd say people will be fine if they hold together.
S4.think: She thinks very little changes for her since she'd be at home with her husband and grandchildren. She'd become a storyteller of the old trade.
S4.do: Retires when planned, trains apprentices until then and keeps the family savings safe. Encourages her children and grandchildren to stay close to the land and to church, and leaves the new technology alone.
S4.feel: Uneasy: safe herself, but sorry for what's lost.
S4.quote: A robot can fix a line, but it can't bring soup to a frozen crew at midnight, and I'd like to think that's still worth something.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her own situation is safe, but she still grieves for a way of life. She admits she doesn't know what her grandchildren's lives will look like. Her hope rests on people still needing each other, not on technology or policy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It would take everything out here at once, before anyone could get ready. What would help is companies keeping their apprenticeship schemes and looking after the people who've given them their working lives, and churches and families having time to pull together. Not handouts, people need work, not cheques.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people out here will get through whatever comes because they believe in something bigger than a machine. I'd want people to remember that, when they're making their plans in the city.

headlineQuote: I'd be the old woman telling the grandchildren that once upon a time, a person climbed up there and fixed it with her hands.
portrait: Daria Ibrahim is a 58-year-old line crew leader in farm country who has trained eleven apprentices, keeps a flip phone on principle and says a quiet prayer before every shift. She's traditional, distrustful of big companies and new gadgets, and believes in family, land, church and work rather than government help. Her savings, paid-off house and family land keep her money safe, so she's calm in the plateau and uneasy in steady change, worried mainly about the apprentice programme. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because it would hollow out her whole rural community at once, while longer timelines let her retire on her own terms but still grieve for a way of life.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, because it would take everything in her rural community at once, before anyone could get ready.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping apprenticeship schemes and looking after long-serving workers, and time for churches and families to pull together; work, not cheques.
